Scoring

Game StrategyDivisibility
Game: Take turns with the computer sliding counters left; whoever moves the last counter onto square 0 wins.
How to play: Click a pile, then a lit square up to Max Step places to its left. You go first.

Look for the math

Scoring is the doorway into the theory of impartial games: both players have the same moves, so a position, not a player, is good or bad. Number the squares from 0 on the left and let M be the Max Step.

One counter

From square 0 nothing can move, so the player to move has lost. From squares 1 to M you win in one move. From square M+1 every move lands on 1..M, handing the win to the other player. Carrying on, the losing squares for the player to move (the P-positions) are exactly 0, M+1, 2(M+1), …, the multiples of M+1. Winning means always moving to one of them.

The mex rule

With several counters, give each square a value by the mex rule: g(0) = 0, and g(t) is the smallest number not among the values of the squares you can reach from t. That gives g(t) = t mod (M+1): 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3, … for M = 3. Hint → Modular shows it as dots.

Adding games: the nim-sum

The Sprague–Grundy theorem says that several counters together behave like a game of Nim with heaps g(t): the position is lost for the player to move exactly when the xor (nim-sum) g(t₁) ^ g(t₂) ^ … is 0. Two counters on the same square cancel out, which is why copying your opponent's moves wins then. The logic test solved the game outright for every Max Step, strips of up to 12 squares and up to three counters, and found the rule true every time.

How the computer plays

When the nim-sum is not 0 the computer moves one counter to make it 0, and from then on it cannot lose. When the nim-sum is already 0 it has no good move and slides the leftmost free counter a random distance. So you can win only by reaching a nim-sum of 0 and keeping it there.

Start with one counter and Hint on Forward or Modular. Which squares do you want to leave the counter on?
